subtopic: Gaming versus homework

passage: In the school counsellor's room, Mridul sat beside his mother, looking at his shoes. His marks had dropped, and he knew why. "I sit down to study," he told the counsellor, "and the tablet is right there. I tell myself two minutes, and it's forty." The counsellor asked, "What would help?" Mridul thought. "If it isn't in the room, I can't pick it up." He turned to his mother. "Ammi, can you keep the tablet from six to eight? In your cupboard. Even if I ask, don't give it." His mother raised her eyebrows. "Your idea?" "Mine." His friend Eshaan, waiting outside, heard the plan on the way to the bus and laughed. "You're making your mum your guard?" "I'm making her my helper," Mridul said.

qa.a: Eshaan laughs at it, seeing Ammi as a guard rather than a helper.

subtopic: Gaming versus homework
subtype: Approach: asking a parent to hold the device [Action]
passage: I'm Sonali, Ishwar's sister. Last month Ishwar kept saying he was studying, but every time I walked past his door I heard the little ping of his game. "Because when it's near me, I can't stop." Mummy put it in her handbag. At seven-thirty Ishwar came out and asked for it "just to check one thing". Mummy said, "You told me not to give it." qa.q: How does Sonali see the rule?
qa.a: Sonali notices his better marks and that he keeps handing the tablet over, though unsure whether he likes it.

grounding: A sister watches a boy hand his tablet to their mother during study time, a limit he chose because he found it hard to stop.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: owning up straight away [Action]
passage: The ball flew off Jeevan's bat, over the neem tree and straight through Urmila-amma's kitchen window. Crash. The other boys in the village lane scattered. Jeevan stood frozen, bat in hand. He could run too; nobody had seen who hit it. Instead he went home and found his father mending a fishing net on the verandah. "Appa, I broke Urmila-amma's window." His father put the net down. "Then let's go." At her door Jeevan's voice shook. "Amma, it was my shot. I'm sorry. I'll give my savings towards the glass." Urmila-amma looked at him for a long moment, then laughed. "My sons broke that same window three times. Your father and I will sort out the glass. You sweep up the pieces, and hit the next one the other way."

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel at Urmila-amma's door?

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Going straight to his father and then to her door, because owning up at once showed honesty that made her kind rather than angry.

qa.q: How does Urmila-amma see the broken window?
qa.a: More amused than angry, remembering her own sons breaking the same window.

grounding: After breaking a neighbour's window, a boy owns up at once with his father, offers to help pay, and finds the neighbour kind.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: owning up straight away [Action]
passage: In their street in Auckland, Wei was practising cricket against the garage when a bad bounce sent the ball into Mrs Kowalski's front window. The glass cracked in a star. Wei's stomach dropped. Mrs Kowalski was known on the street for complaining about noise. He thought about hiding the ball and saying nothing. Instead he went inside to his dad, who was cooking dumplings. "Dad, I cracked Mrs Kowalski's window." His dad turned off the stove. "Come on, then." At her door Wei said, "It was me. I'm really sorry. I can pay some of the glass from my savings." Mrs Kowalski looked at the crack, then at him. "You came to tell me yourself? Most people wouldn't." She smiled. "Your father and I will sort it. You can help me wash my windows on Saturday."

qa.a: He was afraid of Mrs Kowalski's anger, since she was known for complaining.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling his dad and knocking on her door straight away, because it showed respect and made her willing to be kind.

qa.q: How does Mrs Kowalski see Wei's visit?
qa.a: She is surprised and impressed that he came himself, and responds kindly.

grounding: A boy who cracks a neighbour's window with a cricket ball owns up straight away with his father and finds her kind.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: imagining the consequences of each choice [Thinking]
passage: Last year at my friend Lalremsiami's house, I knocked a pen over and a blob of ink landed on her parents' cream sofa. I'm Indu. My first thought was to push a cushion over it and go home. Nobody had seen. Then I thought it through. Her mother would find it. She'd ask Siami. Siami would say, "Indu was sitting there." Then I'd be the girl who ruined the sofa and hid it, and maybe I'd never be invited again. If I told now, there might be a scolding, but her mother would still trust me in their house. subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake

passage: On Tuesday, in the Class 5 library period, Omkar pulled the atlas out too fast and a page tore right across India. He looked around. The librarian, Mahima-ma'am, was stamping books at her desk. Omkar slid the atlas behind the thick dictionaries on the bottom shelf and walked out. For three days he couldn't stop thinking about it. At lunch he pushed his food around. When he passed the library, he walked faster. On Friday Mahima-ma'am stopped him at the door with the atlas in her hands. "Omkar, you had this on Tuesday. Do you know what happened to this page?" His ears went hot. "I tore it," he whispered. "I was scared." She nodded. "Next time, bring it to me. Tape is easier than hiding."

qa.a: Behind the thick dictionaries on the bottom shelf.

qa.a: Taken the atlas straight to Mahima-ma'am, so it could be taped at once.

qa.a: Calmly and practically, pointing out that tape is easier than hiding.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake

Art room note, Thursday.
During the painting lesson, Sangeeta knocked her water jar across Priya's finished drawing of a peacock. Priya burst into tears. Sangeeta said "Sorry" at once, but I could see that saying it didn't satisfy her. She asked if she could stay back at lunch. For forty minutes she sat with a fresh sheet and Priya's smudged drawing beside it, copying the peacock's outline carefully, then asked Priya to come and colour it with her. When Priya arrived, the outline was ready and neat. They painted the feathers together. Sangeeta told me, "Sorry doesn't give her the drawing back. This does." I have put both drawings, the smudged one and the new one, on the class board.
Dilnaz, art teacher

qa.q: What did Sangeeta knock over?
qa.a: Her water jar.

qa.q: Why wasn't saying sorry enough for Sangeeta?
qa.a: She felt guilty and knew that words alone would not give Priya her drawing back.

qa.q: What else could Sangeeta have done if there was no time at lunch?
qa.a: Offered to redraw it at home and bring it the next day, still repairing the harm.

qa.q: How might Priya feel arriving at lunch?
qa.a: Surprised and comforted to find the outline ready and a friend to paint with.

grounding: An art teacher's note records a girl who spoiled a classmate's drawing apologising and redrawing it, seeing repair as more than words.

Today I spoilt Simran's drawing for the competition. I leaned on it with my elbow while it was still wet, and the whole sky smudged into the mountains. Simran didn't cry, but she went very quiet, and that was worse. I said sorry about five times. It didn't feel like enough. Sorry doesn't fix a sky. subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake

Day-care note, Monday.
Farhan came back from the playground twenty minutes late today. When I asked, he said, "I was at the playground, Usha-aunty." That was true; I had seen him there. But his shoes were covered in the grey mud found only on the canal path, the path all the children have been told not to use because the edge is broken. I asked him gently, "Which way did you come back?" He looked away and said, "The normal way," then, after a moment, "Mostly." He had not lied exactly, but he had left out the part that mattered. I sat with him and explained that the unsafe part is exactly what adults need to know. I have called his mother today, and tomorrow I will walk the children back myself.
Usha, day-care

qa.q: How late was Farhan?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Farhan have felt when he said 'Mostly'?
qa.a: Uneasy and guilty, knowing he had left out the canal path.

qa.q: What else could Farhan have said?
qa.a: The whole truth about the canal path, so the adults could keep him safe.

qa.q: How does Usha see Farhan's half-truth?
qa.a: Usha sees that it hid the one part that mattered, and takes protective steps the same day.

grounding: A carer's note records a boy who tells a true but partial account, hiding that he used a forbidden, unsafe path.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake

His face went red, then slowly calmed. He said, "You told me yourself. Now work." And Gopika-chechi kept her word for a whole term.
